title: Trump: Rudy Giuliani asks DHS to seize voting machines
description_short: Trump: Rudy Giuliani asks DHS to seize voting machines
description_medium: In December 2020, Rudy Giuliani asked DHS official Ken Cuccinelli whether the department could seize voting machines as part of efforts to challenge the election result. Cuccinelli told him DHS lacked that authority. The linked reporting describes a request, not a completed seizure, and places it within the broader push to overturn Trump’s defeat.
description_long:
Rudy Giuliani contacted Ken Cuccinelli in December 2020 to ask whether the Department of Homeland Security could seize voting machines. Cuccinelli, serving in the department’s senior leadership, responded that DHS did not have authority to do so. The linked timeline cites reporting that placed Giuliani’s proposal within efforts to overturn the presidential election result.

DHS oversees the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, whose work includes protecting election infrastructure. That protective role did not provide the seizure power Giuliani was seeking, according to the reported response. The distinction is central to the event: an agency’s connection to election security is not equivalent to a general power to take possession of state and local voting equipment at a campaign lawyer’s request. The supplied record establishes the proposal and its rejection, rather than an actual federal confiscation. It does not establish that the machines contained evidence sufficient to change the result, or that the request produced another operational action.

title: Donald Trump found guilty on 34 felony counts
description_short: Donald Trump found guilty on 34 felony counts
description_medium: On May 30, 2024, a Manhattan jury convicted Trump on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records. The case concerned records tied to reimbursement of Michael Cohen for a payment to Stormy Daniels before the 2016 election. The linked account describes the later unconditional discharge, which imposed no imprisonment, fine or probation without erasing the conviction.
description_long:
On May 30, 2024, a Manhattan jury found Trump guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records following a trial lasting about six weeks. The case concerned a $130,000 payment made by Michael Cohen to Stormy Daniels before the 2016 election and the records used when Trump reimbursed Cohen. Prosecutors argued that the payment sought to prevent political damage and that recording reimbursements as legal expenses concealed the arrangement.

The linked account identifies the counts as covering invoices, ledger entries and checks, rather than 34 separate payments to Daniels. The verdict made Trump the first former U.S. president convicted of felony crimes. The timeline also records a later sentencing development: on January 10, 2025, he received an unconditional discharge. That meant no imprisonment, fines or probation, while leaving the conviction in place. The event should be distinguished from other criminal or civil cases involving Trump, and the verdict does not adjudicate every allegation made about his personal conduct.

title: Trump: Jack Smith steps down following Trump case dismissals
description_short: Trump: Jack Smith steps down following Trump case dismissals
description_medium: Jack Smith resigned as special counsel before Trump’s January 2025 inauguration, after the federal cases he brought against Trump had been dismissed before trial. The linked account distinguishes the classified-documents dismissal from the election-case dismissal following Trump’s victory. Smith also submitted a final report, whose release became a separate legal and political dispute.
description_long:
Jack Smith resigned as special counsel before Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration. The linked timeline dates his departure to January 10 and says the news emerged in a footnote in court filings. Attorney General Merrick Garland had appointed him in November 2022 to supervise investigations involving classified documents and efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

The cases ended through different procedures. The classified-documents case was dismissed after Judge Aileen Cannon ruled against the constitutional basis of Smith’s appointment. After Trump won the 2024 election, Smith sought dismissal of the election case under the Justice Department’s policy against prosecuting a sitting president. Neither termination amounted to a trial acquittal resolving all underlying evidence. Smith submitted a final report before departing, and Trump’s lawyers opposed its release. The entry therefore records the conclusion of the special-counsel tenure and the procedural setting, while keeping the report dispute, merits of the allegations and concerns about future retaliation distinct.

title: Trump admin closes DHS / ICE oversight offices
description_short: Trump admin closes DHS / ICE oversight offices
description_medium: On May 23, 2025, employees of three DHS oversight offices were suspended and given separation dates. The offices handled civil rights, immigration-service complaints and detention oversight. DHS characterized the changes as reform, while former personnel questioned whether the remaining staffing could provide meaningful oversight. The linked account describes the practical shutdown and proposed reduced staffing, rather than a congressional repeal of every office.
description_long:
On May 23, 2025, the Trump administration suspended employees and issued separation dates at three Department of Homeland Security oversight offices: Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman, and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman. The linked account describes these personnel measures as effectively shutting down their work.

DHS defended its approach as reform aimed at mismanagement and overlapping responsibilities. The timeline, citing CNN, reports extremely limited staffing during the transition and discusses plans for a small detention-ombudsman team. Former office leader Michelle Brané questioned whether such staffing could meet oversight needs as detention expanded. The account also points to a budget request providing no funding for that office. Those are separate forms of evidence about personnel, planned funding and operational capacity. They do not show that Congress formally repealed every statutory responsibility. The episode concerns the weakening of mechanisms for complaints and scrutiny inside DHS, without establishing that every subsequent detention problem resulted from these specific staff removals.
